Use the per-user installation for setup without administrator rights; see the [installation notes](#install) for unsigned-app warnings and the all-users option. > > **Experienced users** can grab the portable zip, use the [command-line options](#command-line), or [build it from source](#build) with `make` or `build.bat`. > > **Like it?** BatteryHub is free and open source. If it saves you a trip into vendor software, you can support it on [Ko-fi](https://ko-fi.com/krisgfx), [PayPal](https://www.paypal.com/paypalme/krisgfx) or [GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors/krisgfx9). It helps me keep my apps free alongside my studies. Not able to donate? A ⭐ star, sharing it, or reporting an unsupported device with a `--dump` helps just as much. - **Tiny**: a ~350 KB app using about 2 MB of RAM. It's plain C++/Win32, with no runtime and no background service, and supports per-user installation without administrator rights. - **Vendor apps usually aren't required**: most drivers query devices directly. Some headsets use the bundled [HeadsetControl](https://github.com/Sapd/HeadsetControl) helper. Device-specific setup, firmware patches and conflicts with vendor apps are described in the table and [Limitations](#limitations). - **Many brands**: Logitech, Razer, SteelSeries, Corsair, HyperX, Glorious, Jabra, JBL, PlayStation and Xbox controllers, Samsung Galaxy Buds, any Bluetooth device Windows knows a battery level for, and every headset the bundled [HeadsetControl](https://github.com/Sapd/HeadsetControl) supports. ## Display **On the taskbar (default):** `🎧 30% 🖱 93%` next to the notification area, drawn with the Windows icon font. - **Low battery:** a red number means 15% or less. - **Charging:** a blue ⚡ appears next to the number. Once the device is fully charged and still on power, it turns into a green ✓. - **Asleep:** dimmed text means the device is asleep and the last known value is shown. Turn off *Dim sleeping devices* in the menu to keep that value at full brightness. - **Disconnected (optional):** turn on *Show disconnected devices* to display a dimmed `×` for devices whose driver explicitly reports an offline wireless link. This does not infer disconnection from a missed battery poll; the default remains to hide offline devices. - **Two devices of one kind:** with two mice (or two controllers...) both would get the same icon, so each one gets a tiny caption of up to 3 letters in the corner of its icon, taken from its name (`MX`, `PRO`), or a number when the names do not tell them apart. A device that is alone in its kind shows no caption. - **Theme:** it follows light/dark mode and DPI scaling. - **Transparent taskbar themes** (e.g. Windhawk's Taskbar Styler): turn on *Background behind taskbar text* in the menu to keep the text readable over the wallpaper. - **Several monitors:** the widget shows on every monitor's taskbar, next to its clock, so it stays visible while a game runs fullscreen. *Show the widget on* in the menu picks *All monitors*, *Main monitor only*, or one display (e.g. only *Display 3*). - **More display options:** *Icons above percentages* stacks each icon over its level to save width; *Brand colors* shows known brands in their color (Razer green, HyperX red, ...) with a small level bar; two devices of the same kind get a tiny caption so they can be told apart; left and right taskbars get a column of devices. - **Languages:** English, العربية, Deutsch, Español, فارسی, Français, עברית, 日本語, 한국어, Magyar, Polski, Português (Brasil), Русский, Svenska, Tiếng Việt, ภาษาไทย, Türkçe, Українська, 简体中文 and 繁體中文. The app follows the Windows display language; *Language* in the menu picks another one. See [Translations](#translations) to add or improve a language. - **Brand colors:** devices of 15 known brands get their maker's color, with a soft glow and a thin level bar under the percentage: Razer green, Logitech blue, SteelSeries orange, Corsair yellow, HyperX / ROG / ZOWIE red, PlayStation, Xbox, Samsung, Apple, Jabra, JBL, Cooler Master and Steam. Each color has a dark- and a light-taskbar shade. The brand comes from the driver that found the device, then the vendor ID, then the name; colors and rules are in `src/brands.cpp`. Turn it off with *Brand colors* in the menu. **Tray icons:** one icon per device with the number drawn in it, plus a "Low battery" notification at 15%. The app switches to this automatically when the taskbar is vertical or can't be found. **Custom device names:** open the device submenu and select *Rename device...* to set a name (up to 64 characters). The name is shown in the taskbar widget's tooltip/caption, tray tooltip and notifications, and the device menu. Use *Reset to original name* to restore the driver's name. Names are stored locally in the current user's Windows registry (`Software\WirelessBattery`, `DeviceAliases`), using the stable device key. Renaming never changes driver matching, protocol queries, or `--list` / `--dump` diagnostic output. No account or network access is needed. Hover for details. Click for the menu: every device (click one to hide or show it), display mode, *Refresh now*, *Start with Windows*, and *Exit*. Levels refresh every 60 seconds (*Check battery every* in the menu changes this), and right away when a device is plugged in or the PC wakes up. ## Smart Battery Alerts (experimental) You can set a **per-device low-battery notification threshold** from each device's submenu: **Battery alerts** → *Use default (15%)*, *Disable notifications*, or one of 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 30%, 35%, 40%. The existing 15% default stays unchanged unless you choose an override. Settings are stored by device key in the current user's Windows registry (`Software\WirelessBattery`, `AlertThresholds`). An alert is triggered only from a real, fresh 0–100% battery reading when the device is connected, awake and not charging. An alert is issued once, and will re-arm after the level climbs more than 10 percentage points above the chosen threshold (or when charging begins). Missing readings or sleeping devices do not retrigger alerts. Hidden devices don't produce notifications. Disabling notifications for one device does not hide it or change its percentage. Both taskbar-widget and tray-icon modes support notifications. Since Windows needs a notification-area icon to display a legacy balloon, widget mode may show a temporary notification icon for up to one minute after an alert. Widget colours and the low-battery highlight still use the project's original global 15% threshold, independently of the notification setting. ## Battery history & insights Right-click a device in the taskbar widget or tray menu and choose **Battery history...**. The native, DPI-aware viewer (it follows the Windows light/dark theme) shows recorded battery levels with connected sample lines over the last **24 hours**, **7 days**, or **30 days**, along with the latest reading, lowest/highest level, change in percentage points, and sample count. You can clear the selected device's history from the viewer. History is recorded **locally only** for connected, awake devices reporting a numeric percentage. Readings are sampled at most once every 30 minutes per device (except charging-state transitions, with a 60-second minimum). Data is kept for up to 30 days and the local file is kept under about 2 MB. The app never probes hardware beyond its existing polling, sends no history data over the network, and makes a conservative, approximate time-to-empty estimate from recent discharge observations only. At least four points, two hours, a three-percentage-point decline, a fresh reading and a stable discharge segment are required. Charging, old readings or insufficient data suppress the estimate; device-reported runtime is not available. The estimate is not a guarantee. Missing chart data is shown as gaps, not interpolated. Turn off **Record battery history** in the menu to stop saving readings; what was already saved stays until you clear it in the viewer. The file is stored in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\WirelessBattery\battery_history.tsv`. Its device identities are encoded (not encrypted); the file is local to your Windows account. In `--demo`, the chart uses synthetic data that is never saved. **Note:** history starts collecting only after this feature is installed and the app has been running for a while. ## Supported devices Match your model, receiver VID:PID, connection mode and any firmware requirements to the table; `BatteryHub.exe --dump` shows the IDs. A brand name alone does not confirm support for every model. Hardware-test labels apply only to the stated devices and behaviors. Drawing tablets are skipped automatically. ## Updates on Windows Official stable Windows builds check the project's latest published stable release in the background, 30 seconds after startup and then every 24 hours while the app is running. Open the menu to see **Update available: vX.Y.Z...**, or choose **Check for updates...** yourself. Update information appears only in this menu: battery icons, percentages and tooltips stay the same, and automatic checks never show a notification or dialog. Turn off **Automatically check for updates** in the menu to disable background checks. For an installed copy, click the update entry and **Download and install**. Nothing is installed without that click. The app downloads the release's `SHA256SUMS.txt` and its signature, checks the signature against the maintainer's public key built into the app, downloads the Windows installer, and runs it only if its SHA-256 is the one in the signed list (and the one GitHub lists for it). It then updates the existing installation. Settings and startup preference are preserved, and the app reopens after installation. An installation for all users can ask for administrator permission. **Release notes** opens the official release page; **Later** keeps your current version. Portable copies offer the release page for downloading the ZIP manually. Checks contact GitHub's public API without an account or token. No device or battery information is sent. Offline failures and GitHub rate limits leave battery monitoring running; a previously found release stays in the menu until a successful check supersedes it or it is installed. Cancelling a download waits for the current network operation to finish its finite timeout. The installer never restarts Windows automatically. **Why updates are safe to install:** the signing key never goes to GitHub. The maintainer signs each release's checksum list on their own PC (see [docs/releasing.md](docs/releasing.md)), so even someone who took over the GitHub account or its build workflow could not publish an update the app would install. A release without a valid signature is shown in the menu but can only be downloaded by hand. The signature does not replace Windows' own SmartScreen or UAC prompts. Install the first release containing this feature manually once. Development/test builds disable official update checks so local changes cannot be replaced accidentally. Updates for Linux and automatic replacement of portable copies are deferred. ## Command line ``` BatteryHub.exe --list # print every device and its battery level, then exit BatteryHub.exe --json # print a JSON array of devices and battery levels, then exit BatteryHub.exe --dump # every HID collection, HID devices that could not be opened, all USB devices (also ones # without a HID interface) and Bluetooth devices; also saved to %TEMP%\BatteryHub-dump.txt BatteryHub.exe --report # open the "Request support for a device" window BatteryHub.exe --demo # sample devices of every brand instead of real ones (screenshots, checking colors) BatteryHub.exe --quit # close the running instance ``` The Linux build uses the same flags with `wireless-battery` instead of `BatteryHub.exe`, and also accepts `--help`. `--json` prints a stable array that scripts and bar widgets can parse: ```json [{"key":"kysona:373B:1085","name":"CX Wireless mouse","via":"2.4 GHz receiver","kind":"mouse", "percent":85,"level":"","detail":"","charging":false,"asleep":false,"connected":true, "millivolts":4029,"graceSec":1800}] ``` `graceSec` is how long the app keeps showing the last known level while the device is asleep. Adding new fields is backwards compatible. **Device not shown?** Right-click the widget or tray icon and choose **Request support for a device...**. Pick the device, check what will be sent (it is shown word for word: the device name, its type, its USB/HID ids and interface layout, and your optional name and notes) and click **Send**. It goes on the public list at [krisgfx.com/tools](https://krisgfx.com/tools/#requested) and opens or updates a GitHub issue. **Copy full report** puts the complete `--dump` on the clipboard for the issue. Report data is sent only when you click Send. Official Windows builds can also contact GitHub to check for updates, as described in [Updates on Windows](#updates-on-windows); update checks do not send device or battery information. ## Build You need [MinGW-w64](https://www.mingw-w64.org/), e.g. from [MSYS2](https://www.msys2.org/) (`pacman -S mingw-w64-x86_64-gcc make`). ``` make # development build, version 0.0.0 build.bat # plain cmd with g++ and windres on PATH make VERSION=1.2.3 CHANNEL=test # versioned build, official updates disabled build.bat 1.2.3 test # equivalent versioned cmd build make test VERSION=1.2.3 CHANNEL=test # device and updater regression tests ``` To build the installer and portable zip, install [Inno Setup](https://jrsoftware.org/isinfo.php), first build with the intended version (for example `make VERSION=1.2.3 CHANNEL=test`), then run `powershell -File installer\build-installer.ps1 -Version 1.2.3`. Packaging rejects a version that differs from the executable. It downloads the pinned HeadsetControl release and verifies its checksum. GitHub Actions does all of this automatically: pushing a tag like `v1.0.0` publishes a release with the installer, the portable zip and the HeadsetControl source (as its GPL license requires). Windows builds also need PowerShell for generating the shared executable/resource version. The official repository's version tags build with `CHANNEL=stable`; local builds default to `dev`. Forks and pull requests do not enable official updates automatically. `BatteryHub.exe` on its own also works. Without `headsetcontrol.exe` next to it (or on `PATH`) you just lose the extra headsets. ## Linux (experimental) A Linux build sits alongside the Windows app. It uses the same vendor drivers with a hidraw-based HID backend and a GTK4 StatusNotifierItem tray icon; the Windows code path is unchanged. All Linux-only files are in `linux/` and `src/linux/`, and `build-linux.sh` builds it (Windows keeps using `build.bat`). | | Fedora | Ubuntu / Debian | |---|---|---| | Compiler & make | `sudo dnf install gcc-c++ make` | `sudo apt install g++ make` | | GTK4 + Cairo | `sudo dnf install gtk4-devel cairo-devel` | `sudo apt install libgtk-4-dev libcairo2-dev` | No extra HID library is needed (hidraw is used directly). ```sh ./build-linux.sh ./build-linux.sh test # unit test for the HID report-descriptor parser ./wireless-battery --list # print detected levels and exit ./wireless-battery --dump # list HID collections ./wireless-battery --quit # close the running tray instance ``` HID access needs a udev rule, otherwise the app starts but finds no devices: ```sh sudo cp linux/70-wireless-battery.rules /etc/udev/rules.d/ sudo udevadm control --reload-rules && sudo udevadm trigger # log out and back in ``` If you previously installed `99-wireless-battery.rules`, remove the old file from `/etc/udev/rules.d/` before reloading the rules. The `70-` prefix ensures that `uaccess` is applied before systemd's `73-seat-late.rules` assigns device permissions. The tray icon works natively on KDE Plasma; GNOME needs an AppIndicator host such as `gnome-shell-extension-appindicator`. The optional launcher is `linux/wireless-battery.desktop` (install it plus `linux/wireless-battery.svg` and the binary into `~/.local/`). Phase 1 covers Logitech, Razer, SteelSeries, Corsair, HyperX, PlayStation, Cooler Master, Glorious, Finalmouse, Keychron, Ninjutso, Rapoo, Zebronics (3554:FC0A) and the shared Kysona/Pulsar/ATK/G-Wolves protocols. Bluetooth/UPower fallbacks, HeadsetControl and the remaining vendors are planned follow-up phases. ## Limitations - **Crowded taskbars:** with a very full centered Windows 11 taskbar, the app buttons can reach the widget. On Windows 10 the task-button area is narrowed automatically. - **Phones:** read from a file Phone Link writes for the Start menu companion card, which is not a documented API and may change with Phone Link updates. The phone shows while Phone Link reports it as connected; a card older than 3 hours is shown dimmed. The card also says when the phone is charging, which shows as the charging bolt. - **Razer HyperSpeed Multi-Device:** compatible receivers can report the mouse and keyboard separately, even when one sleeps. See [receiver protocol and tested hardware](docs/razer_hyperspeed.md). - **Sleeping devices:** a device that is asleep may not answer. Its last value stays visible, dimmed unless *Dim sleeping devices* is turned off in the menu. Logitech receivers drop sleeping devices from the link, so their last value is kept for 30 minutes. - **Logitech mice on the `046D:C542` receiver** (C-U0019 "Wireless Receiver", shipped with the M280 and some M185 / M190 / M220): this receiver does not speak HID++. It exposes only a standard mouse and one vendor feature report (ID 5, 7 bytes), with no HID++ short or long reports, so the Logitech driver has nothing to ask and the mouse is not listed. [Solaar](https://github.com/pwr-Solaar/Solaar/issues/1835) does not support it for the same reason, and no battery query for it is documented. - **HECATE G2 Wireless 7.1 headset** (2.4 GHz dongle `35BB:A009` / `A209`): no battery query for its dongle is documented yet, so it is not read. A USB capture while the HECATE software shows the headset battery (see CONTRIBUTING.md) is the way to add it. - **Keychron keyboards:** with stock firmware they only report their battery over Bluetooth (shown via the Bluetooth support). Over the 2.4 GHz receiver or the cable they need firmware with the battery patch ([docs/keychron_keyboard_firmware/README.md](docs/keychron_keyboard_firmware/README.md)); updating the keyboard from Keychron Launcher removes it. Keychron mice are supported. - **Baseus AeQur GH02 headset:** the 2.4 GHz dongle (`10D6:4802`, Actions chip) only carries audio, media keys and the chip's firmware-update channel, not the battery. Connect the headset over Bluetooth to see its level (shown via the Bluetooth support when Windows reports one). - **Weikav Lucky65 v1 keyboard:** the firmware does not report its battery over the 2.4 GHz dongle (`0603:0351`, Novatek chip). The keyboard has no battery-check shortcut, and the official configurator only connects over the USB cable, not through the dongle, so there is no battery reading to show. - **Rapoo:** supported VT mice push their status, so a refresh can wait up to 4 seconds per matching interface. Sleeping mice may stay dimmed with their last reading for up to 30 minutes. Support is for Nordic 54L report `07` and legacy `BB` (VT3 Pro, VT1 Pro Max); CH584 report `08`, office MT/M-series mice and other firmware protocols are not covered by this driver. - **GameSir Cyclone Pro:** the dongle carries no battery level, so it is read from the pad over Bluetooth LE. Pair the pad with Windows once (Settings > Bluetooth & devices > Add device > Bluetooth > `GameSir-Cyclone Pro`), and keep playing through the dongle. The PC needs Bluetooth. The level refreshes every 2 minutes, and there is no percentage while charging. Without pairing, the dongle shows as an Xbox controller at "Full". Details in [docs/gamesir_cyclone_pro.md](docs/gamesir_cyclone_pro.md). - **RAWM:** the mouse is asked through its receiver, so a sleeping mouse does not answer; it stays dimmed with its last reading for up to 30 minutes and adds about a second to a refresh while it sleeps. Only the Leviathan V4 on the RAWM HS Receiver (`1915:2346`) is tested; the other models are taken from RAWM HUB's device table. The Leviathan V4 GT and NYX60 (VID `373E`, RAWM HUB 3.0) and the RAWM HS keyboards use other protocols and are not covered. - **Flydigi:** this driver targets Vader 5 Pro and Apex 5; Bluetooth and other Flydigi models (for example Apex 6) are not covered. Percentages represent coarse battery levels. Apex 5 was tested on real hardware over the 2.4 GHz receiver and a USB cable; Vader 5 Pro follows SDL and Windows hardware traces. - **Not supported yet:** MSI devices outside the models listed in the table, Razer Kraken headsets, Barracuda models other than the Barracuda X (2022) (`1532:054E` / `0550` / `0552`) and Barracuda Pro (`1532:053A`), HyperX Pulsefire mice other than the Haste 2 Wireless / Haste 2 Core Wireless / Haste 2 Mini / Dart, and the Xbox Wireless Headset on the Xbox adapter are not covered by the current drivers. The Xbox Wireless Headset works over Bluetooth. A USB capture from an owner (see CONTRIBUTING.md) can help add support. - **Other devices:** some 2.4 GHz devices use undocumented protocols and are not supported yet. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for how to help add one. ## How it works Each vendor driver in [`src/drivers/`](src/drivers) recognises its devices by USB vendor and product ID, and only ever sends read-only battery queries. Unknown devices are never written to. The generic fallbacks (HID battery usage, Bluetooth, XInput, HeadsetControl) only look at devices no vendor driver has claimed. The taskbar widget is a layered child window of `Shell_TrayWnd`, placed left of `TrayNotifyWnd`. If Explorer restarts, it is re-created. ## Translations Every language is a plain UTF-8 text file in [`lang/`](lang): English on the left, the translation on the right. ``` @code = it @name = Italiano Refresh now = Aggiorna ora {name} is at {percent}% = {name} è al {percent}% ``` - **Use your own language right away:** choose *Language → Add your own language...* in the menu. It opens `%APPDATA%\WirelessBattery\lang` with `_template.txt`, which lists every phrase. Copy it to e.g. `it.txt`, fill in `@code`, `@name` and the translations, and the language appears in the menu (no restart needed). A file there with the same `@code` as a built-in language replaces its phrases, so you can also fix a single word locally. - **Share it with everyone:** send the file as a pull request to [`lang/`](lang). The build includes every file in that folder automatically; no code change is needed. - Keep `{placeholders}` as they are, and add `@rtl = 1` for right-to-left scripts. Phrases left empty stay English, so a partial translation is fine. - The `--list` and `--dump` output stays English on purpose: it is pasted into GitHub issues. ## Credits App icon by [nik-txt](https://github.com/nik-txt) ([`res/app.svg`](res/app.svg)).
